lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Name two net-game rules that keep play fair.

FEEDBACK
e.g. rotate serve; replay let; no body contact — any two.

WATCH FOR
Smashing at someone’s head on purpose is unsafe.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Learn rules of a modified net game and teach a peer three rules + one safety point.

Write a short reflection naming one choice you changed and why. Any movement is optional, adult-supervised and can be done in a gentler way or described instead.

lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Learn rules of a modified net game and teach a peer three rules + one safety point. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: e.g. rotate serve; replay let; no body contact — any two. Reasoning: I used net by attending to rule rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Smashing at someone’s head on purpose is unsafe. Correction: e.g. rotate serve; replay let; no body contact — any two. Why: the correction restores accurate use of net.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with net, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

teach_steps.explain:
Net games use a net/barrier, rules about sending an object over and scoring when opponents cannot return; modified rules keep games inclusive.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make safe, healthy and respectful choices using clear cues and reasons, rather than guessing or copying others. Every choice keeps bodies safe and includes everyone.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the cues, rules or choices that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. For any movement, use a clear space, ask an adult to be nearby, move at your own comfortable level and stop if anything hurts or feels unsafe. You may always choose a gentler version or only describe the movement. One deliberate, reasoned change is more useful than a longer answer.
